Sirach Prologue 1a

but lovers of learning should also be able to benefit those outside, both by speaking and by writing, my grandfather Jesus, having devoted himself extensively to reading the law and the prophets

  1. 2 Timothy 2:2 Learned instruction passed on for others' benefit

    Sirach's translator says lovers of learning should benefit others by speaking and writing, before describing his grandfather's reading. Timothy is instructed to entrust what he heard to faithful people able to teach others. Both make reception of teaching lead to communicating it onward; neither the grandfather Jesus nor the translator is identified with anyone in Timothy.

    Read matching passage

    2 Timothy 2:2 and the things you heard from me through many witnesses, entrust these to faithful people who will be able to teach others also.

Sirach Prologue 1b

and the other ancestral books, and having acquired considerable familiarity with them, was himself moved to write something concerning instruction and wisdom, so that lovers of learning, by becoming engaged with these things too, might advance much further through a life according to the law.

  1. Sirach 50:27 same act

    The prologue says its subject 'was himself moved to write something concerning instruction and wisdom', and Sirach 50:27 says that Jesus son of Sirach 'inscribed instruction in understanding and knowledge in this book' and 'poured wisdom like rain from his heart'. Both describe the writing of a book of instruction and wisdom; 50:27 names its writer.

    Read matching passage

    Sirach 50:27 Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, the Jerusalemite, inscribed instruction in understanding and knowledge in this book; he poured wisdom like rain from his heart.

Sirach Prologue 1f

I myself considered it most necessary to contribute some diligence and hard work toward translating this book. During that time I devoted many wakeful hours and much skill to completing the book and publishing it also for those living abroad who wish to learn,

  1. 2 Maccabees 2:25-27 Sleepless literary labor undertaken for readers

    Sirach's translator reports wakeful hours, skill and hard work to translate and publish for learners abroad. The Maccabees abridger describes sweat and sleeplessness while undertaking difficult literary labor for readers' benefit. The particular parallel is labor and lost sleep to make a work useful to others; translation and abridgment remain distinct tasks and authors.

    Read matching passage

    2 Maccabees 2:25 we have taken thought for the pleasure of those who wish to read, for the ease of those eager to commit it to memory, and for the benefit of everyone who encounters it.

    2 Maccabees 2:26 For us who have undertaken the hard work of abridgement, the task is not easy; it involves sweat and sleeplessness.

    2 Maccabees 2:27 Just as it is not easy for someone preparing a banquet and seeking others’ benefit, nevertheless, for the gratitude of the many, we will gladly bear the hard work.

Closed with no supportable cross-reference

  • Sirach Prologue 1: The translator's opening states that many great things were given to Israel through the law, the prophets and those who followed, so that readers might become knowledgeable. The available texts share only words such as 'knowledgeable', 'since' or 'ought', and no other passage describes this transmission of Israel's writings for instruction and wisdom.
  • Sirach Prologue 1c: The unit is the translator's request that readers read with goodwill and attention and be forgiving where he may seem to fall short. The available texts concern a king urging a mother, a guard's permission to go wherever seems good, or forgiving one's brother, and share only the words urged, attention, seems or forgiving, not an author's appeal to readers.
  • Sirach Prologue 1d: The unit explains that things expressed in Hebrew lack equal force when translated into another language, including the law and prophecies. The available texts mention Paul or a heavenly voice speaking in the Hebrew language, or Christ's equality with God, none of which concerns translation from Hebrew.
  • Sirach Prologue 1e: The unit dates the translator's arrival in Egypt to the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes. The only dated parallel available is the thirty-eighth year of Azariah of Judah, a different king and era, and the remaining texts share only the word likeness; no text refers to Euergetes or this arrival.
  • Sirach Prologue 1g: The unit states that the translated work is meant to prepare readers' character to live according to the law. The available texts use the word character for a messenger, Philip, Onias or proven endurance, and none expresses this purpose of forming life according to the law.
  • Sirach 3:5: The unit promises that one who honors a father will be gladdened by children and heard in prayer. The available texts concern a husband's honor of his wife and unhindered prayer, glory from a father's honor, wine that gladdens, or a king gladdened by God; none joins honoring a father with joy in one's children or answered prayer.
  • Sirach 6:5: The unit says a sweet voice multiplies friends and a well-spoken tongue multiplies friendly greetings. The available texts speak of a yielding answer turning away wrath, gracious speech for answering others, or friends exchanging greetings, but none states that pleasant speech gains friends.
  • Sirach 6:11: The unit describes a fair-weather friend who in prosperity acts like one's equal and speaks freely to one's household slaves. The available texts concern the release and re-enslavement of slaves, spiritual freedom, or unity of slave and free, and share only the word slaves.
  • Sirach 6:22: The unit says wisdom is according to her name and not manifest to many. The available texts speak of wisdom teaching what is hidden and manifest or of Christ and eternal life being manifested; none concerns wisdom's name or her being hidden from many.
  • Sirach 7:7: The unit forbids sinning against a city's population and casting oneself down among the crowd.   • Sirach 7:24: The unit tells a father to attend to his daughters' bodies and not show them a cheerful face. The available texts use 'cheerful' of looking toward heaven, a cheerful giver, or Esther's face before the king, none of which concerns a father's conduct toward daughters.

  • Sirach 11:34: The unit warns that a stranger settled in one's house brings disorder and estranges one from one's own people. The available texts describe a crooked man separating friends, a disorderly retreat, or disorder in a church, and none concerns a stranger lodged in the household.
  • Sirach 12:12: The unit warns against placing an enemy beside oneself or at one's right hand lest he seek one's seat. The available texts describe the seating and station of Solomon's attendants, Christ seated at God's right hand, or a kinsman declining redemption, and share only the words station, seat or right, not this succession danger.
  • Sirach 13:5: The unit describes a wealthy associate who lives with someone who has means and empties him while taking no trouble himself. The available texts share only the words empty, trouble or take in unrelated contexts such as returning the ark, Daniel's preservation or Gehazi's greed.
  • Sirach 13:8: The unit warns against being misled or brought low through one's folly. The available texts speak of prophets misleading the people, assumptions misleading many, idolatry not misleading, or the folly at Gibeah, and share only the words misled or folly.
  • Sirach 13:13: The unit urges great vigilance because one walks alongside one's downfall. The available texts use 'take great care' or 'keep watch' for keeping the law or seeking wisdom, or describe Jesus walking on the sea, and none concerns walking beside one's downfall.
  • Sirach 13:15: The unit says every living creature loves its like and every person his neighbor. The available texts mention sea creatures, a creature molded from clay, or a one-horned creature, and share only the word creature, not the principle of loving one's like.
  • Sirach 13:16: The unit says all flesh gathers according to kind and a man clings to someone like himself. The available texts distinguish kinds of flesh or describe flesh consumed or preserved, but none states the principle of social affinity among like persons.
  • Sirach 14:6: The unit declares no one worse than the one who begrudges himself and introduces the repayment of his evil. The available Proverbs texts warn about dining with or the haste of a begrudging man toward others, and the remaining texts share only the words begrudging or repayment; none concerns begrudging oneself.
  • Sirach 14:7: The unit says the self-begrudging man does good forgetfully and in the end reveals his evil. The available texts concern forgetting luxury in suffering or being a forgetful hearer of the law, and share only words of forgetting and revealing, not this conduct.
  • Sirach 16:9: The unit says God did not have mercy on 'the nation of destruction, those carried away in their sins' without naming that nation. The Deuteronomy texts concern Israel showing no mercy to the nations of Canaan or their destruction for ungodliness, which would require supplying an identification the unit does not state, and the other texts share only words such as destruction, carried or sins.
  • Sirach 16:21: The unit says there is a tempest a person will not see and most of God's works are hidden, within the speech of one who thinks God takes no notice. The Job texts speak of hearing little of God's ways and of thunder and great deeds not known, and the psalms mention tempests in other senses; none shares the unseen tempest or this argumentative setting.
  • Sirach 17:8: The unit says God set His eye upon human hearts to show them the greatness of His works. The available texts praise the greatness of God's works, the heavens recounting His glory, or His invisible qualities seen in creation, but none describes God setting His eye upon hearts.
  • Sirach 18:7: The unit is the paradox that when a person finishes he begins and when he stops he is at a loss. The available texts ask what man is, describe finishing a work, or use 'at a loss' in other settings, and none shares this paradox.
  • Sirach 18:28: The unit says every understanding person has known wisdom and will give acknowledgment to the one who finds her. The available texts speak of God making wisdom known or teaching wisdom, but none concerns acknowledgment given to the one who finds wisdom.
  • Sirach 19:5: The unit says only that the one who rejoices in heart will be condemned. The available texts concern the condemnation of Jesus, condemnation of unbelievers, or the heart condemning us, and none shares this statement about rejoicing in heart.
  • Sirach 20:10: The unit contrasts a gift that does not benefit with a gift whose repayment is double. The available texts mention rulers loving gifts and repayment, Joseph's brothers taking double silver, or the Corban gift, and none shares this contrast between profitless gifts and double return.
  • Sirach 20:12: The unit says someone buys much for little and pays for it sevenfold. The available texts share only the words much, little or someone in unrelated statements, and none describes a purchase repaid sevenfold.
  • Sirach 20:17: The unit says those who eat the fool's bread are base in speech and asks how many will laugh at him. The available texts concern eating the Lord's bread, a stone base under the Sea, or practicing base things, and share only the words bread or base.
  • Sirach 20:23: The unit says someone makes a promise to a friend out of shame and gains him as an enemy for nothing. The available texts speak generally of a friend becoming an enemy, friendship with the world, or acquiring things, but none involves a promise made from shame.
  • Sirach 21:7: The unit contrasts one known far away for power of tongue with the understanding person who knows when he slips. The available texts speak of slips of the tongue, intelligible speech, or wisdom known through speech, but none shares the contrast between distant fame and recognizing one's own slip.
  • Sirach 21:18: The unit says wisdom is like a ruined house to a fool and an uncomprehending person's knowledge is unexamined words. The available Proverbs texts contrast wise and foolish speech or conduct in general terms, and none shares the ruined-house comparison or the unexamined words.
  • Sirach 21:27: The unit says that when an ungodly person curses Satan he curses his own soul. The available texts refer to Satan tempting Jesus, divided against himself, or taking away the word, and none concerns cursing Satan or cursing one's own soul.
  • Sirach 22:26: The unit says that if evil befalls the speaker because of a friend, everyone who hears will guard against him. The available texts describe guards at the crucifixion or tomb, reports of an outrage, or people glorifying God at what happened, and share only the words guard, hear or happen.
  • Sirach 23:12: The unit speaks of 'an expression comparable to death' to be kept from Jacob's inheritance without naming it. The law on naming the Lord's name would require identifying that expression as blasphemy, which the unit does not state, and the other texts share only the words inheritance, depart or sins.
  • Sirach 23:16: The unit is only the numerical introduction 'Two kinds multiply sins, and the third will bring wrath'. It names no sin itself, and the available texts on adultery, sexual immorality, ordered gifts, or multiplied sins and wrath relate only to the examples that follow or share only the counting form.
  • Sirach 25:13: The unit states preferences for any wound but a wound of the heart and any evil but a woman's evil. No text in the edition was found that makes the same comparisons; passages on marital trouble or grief do not share the stated preferences.
  • Sirach 25:14: The unit continues with preferences for any calamity but that from those who hate, and any retribution but that of enemies. The available psalms ask rescue from enemies and those who hate, or lament defeat by them, and share only those common terms, not the comparison of calamities.
  • Sirach 25:15: The unit ranks a snake's head and an enemy's anger as unmatched extremes. The Proverbs sayings concern living with a quarrelsome wife, and the other passages only share the words anger and enemy; none uses the snake's-head comparison or ranks anger this way.
  • Sirach 25:17: The unit's distinctive image is a woman's evil darkening her face like a bear. The Daniel passages describe faces changing from fury or fear, Leviticus concerns a lesion's appearance, and Proverbs 27:15 uses a dripping image; none has the bear comparison.
  • Sirach 25:22: The unit says that wrath, shamelessness and great shame result when a wife supplies her husband. Sirach 26:8 concerns a drunken wife, Sirach 22:4 concerns a daughter, and the Chronicles verses concern Israel's repentance; none addresses a wife's provision for her husband.
  • Sirach 25:25: The unit pairs giving water an outlet with giving an evil wife freedom of speech. Proverbs 17:14 in this edition has no water image. The other passages use freedom or freedom of speech in unrelated senses (before God, Christian liberty, national independence).
  • Sirach 28:15: The unit says a third tongue drove out courageous women and deprived them of their labors. The leads only share isolated words (third, tongue, courageous, labor, deprived), with no saying about slander expelling women or taking their labors.
  • Sirach 28:21: The unit calls the death brought by the tongue an evil death and says Hades is preferable to it. The leads use the word preferable in unrelated comparisons (hope of resurrection; a thief and a liar) and do not compare a death with Hades.
  • Sirach 29:24: The unit describes the grievous life of going from house to house as a guest who cannot open his mouth. The leads share only the words grievous, house, live or guest, in unrelated settings; none describes a dependent guest forced into silence.
  • Sirach 29:28: The unit names rebuke about lodging and a creditor's reproach as burdensome to a prudent person. The leads use the words burdensome or prudence about commandments and wisdom; none concerns lodging, debt or a creditor.
  • Sirach 30:14: The unit prefers a healthy poor person to a rich person scourged in his body. The Proverbs sayings share the better-poor-than-rich form, but their contrast is moral (truth versus lying, righteousness versus deceit), not physical health. The other leads do not make this comparison.
  • Sirach 31:4: The unit contrasts the poor laborer's diminished livelihood and his neediness at rest with the rich laborer before him. The leads speak of the poor and needy in general (not depriving them, injustice to them, God hearing them) and do not describe this outcome of labor and rest.
  • Sirach 33:6: The unit compares a mocking friend to a breeding horse that neighs under every rider. Jeremiah 8:6 compares a runner to a neighing horse, Jeremiah 9:4 speaks of mocking a friend, and the other leads mention friends or horses separately; none combines them in this comparison.
  • Sirach 33:20: Re-reviewed with fresh leads; the proposed link did not survive a second reading: No textual connection: no shared wording, image or person, only a thematic application of Sirach's general advice to the parable. The father in Luke divides property and does not give his son authority over him.
  • Sirach 33:23: The unit urges preeminence in all one's works and keeping one's glory free of blemish. The Hezekiah passages concern setting a house in order before death, which is not this verse's subject, and the New Testament leads use blemish of sacrificial or moral purity before God.
  • Sirach 34:3: The unit describes a dream vision as a likeness of a face opposite a face. Proverbs 27:19 in this edition says faces are not like faces, which is the opposite of a mirror image. The other leads mention dreams, visions or likenesses without this face-to-face image.
  • Sirach 34:11: The unit is the speaker's personal claim that his wandering showed him many things and that his understanding exceeds his words. The leads only share the word exceed, in unrelated contexts (righteousness, divine anger, fire in water).
  • Sirach 36:20: The unit says a twisted heart gives grief and an experienced person will repay it. Sirach 34:9 and 25:6 praise experience without the twisted heart or repayment. 2 Timothy 4:14 concerns the Lord repaying Alexander, and Ecclesiastes 2:1 concerns testing pleasure.
  • Sirach 36:26: The unit asks who will trust a well-girded robber springing from city to city. The leads mention robbers or thieves in unrelated settings (night thieves in Obadiah, a den of robbers, Jesus arrested as a robber), and Deuteronomy shares only the word springing.
  • Sirach 37:3: The unit asks evil thought where it rolled in from to cover the dry land with deceit. Genesis 6:5 and Jeremiah 17:9 speak generally of the evil or depth of the human heart. The others share only cover, deceit or dry land; none uses this image of evil thought covering the land.
  • Sirach 37:5: The unit describes a companion who labors with a friend for his belly's sake and takes up a shield before battle. The Kings verses concern God shielding Jerusalem, and Proverbs 22:24 and Micah 7:5 warn about companions generally; none describes this self-interested companion.
  • Sirach 37:8: The unit warns that a counselor will counsel for himself and may cast a lot against you. The leads concern the counsel of the ungodly, God needing no counselor, foolish royal counselors and divine counsel; none describes a self-interested advisor or the casting of a lot.
  • Sirach 37:11: The unit lists people with a conflict of interest who should not be consulted, such as a woman about her rival or a merchant about exchange. The leads only mention household slaves, hired workers or merchants in laws or sayings about how to treat them, not about consulting them.
  • Sirach 37:14: The unit says a man's soul can report more than seven watchmen on a watchtower. Proverbs 20:27 and 1 Corinthians 2:11 speak of the human spirit's inward knowledge without the watchmen comparison. The other leads mention watchmen or reports in unrelated narratives.
  • Sirach 37:21: The unit says the preceding speaker was not given grace by the Lord because he was deprived of all wisdom. Luke 2:40 and 2 Corinthians 1:12 pair grace and wisdom positively and do not speak of grace withheld for lack of wisdom. The other leads share only the word deprived.
  • Sirach 38:8: The unit says God's works will not end and that peace on the earth comes from Him, in the context of healing and the apothecary. Luke 10:34 shows wound care without this statement, and the Jeremiah and Ezekiel verses concern war and peace in the land.
  • Sirach 38:13: The unit says there is a time when success is also in physicians' hands. The leads concern the Lord granting success in battle or Jason's misguided success, not success in medical practice.
  • Sirach 38:19: The unit says grief remains in calamity and the poor person's life weighs on the heart. The leads mention calamity in prayers, explanations of judgment or a psalm of protection, with no reference to lasting grief or the poor person's life.
  • Sirach 38:25: The unit asks how a plowman occupied with oxen and bulls can become wise. 1 Kings 19:19 and Job 1:14 merely show oxen plowing, Ecclesiastes 12:11 uses goads as an image for wise words, and 1 Chronicles 20:5 mentions a spear shaft; none addresses a farmer's lack of leisure for wisdom.
  • Sirach 38:32: The unit says a city cannot be settled or people sojourn and walk about without the craftsmen just described. The leads share only without, neither or sojourning (Lamentations, Hebrews 7:3, 1 Corinthians 11:11, Esther 4:16) and say nothing about craftsmen sustaining a city.
  • Sirach 39:28: The unit speaks of spirits created for retribution whose scourges God made firm in anger. The psalm verses describe winds, fire and weather obeying God's word without any retributive role, and the other leads share only maker, anger or strength.
  • Sirach 40:14: The unit says that when he opens his hands he will rejoice, while transgressors will cease. The unnamed subject is not identified as a generous giver, so Deuteronomy 15:11 (opening one's hand to the poor) cannot be matched to him. The other leads share only open, rejoice or transgressors.
  • Sirach 40:16: The unit says waterside reed grass will be plucked out before all other grass. Job 8:12 in this edition says every plant withers before it drinks, which is not a before-other-grass comparison. The other leads mention reeds, riverbanks or grass in unrelated settings.
  • Sirach 40:22: The unit ranks the green growth of a crop above grace and beauty desired by the eye. The leads describe green growth or fruitful trees as God's provision but do not compare them with beauty or grace.
  • Sirach 41:20: The unit lists, among things to be ashamed of, wronging the truth of God and His covenant and planting the elbow on bread. Job 31:1 and Matthew 5:28 concern looking at a woman, which is not part of this unit. The other leads share only the words bread, truth or covenant.
  • Sirach 42:2: The unit lists the law of the Most High, His covenant, and a judgment that acquits the ungodly among things not to be ashamed of. Deuteronomy 16:19 forbids perverting judgment, and the prophetic leads say God will not acquit; none states this unit's claim.
  • Sirach 42:6: The unit advises a seal with an evil woman and locks where many hands are present. Bel and Dragon 1:11 seals a temple to test the priests, Job 28:15 mentions locked treasure, and 2 Samuel 13 locks a door behind Tamar; none concerns household safeguards against an evil woman or many hands.
  • Sirach 42:13: The unit compares a moth coming from clothes to a woman's wickedness coming from a woman. The Job leads use moths as images of frailty and decay and draw no comparison about a woman.
  • Sirach 42:14: The unit prefers a man's wickedness to a woman who does good and warns that a shaming woman brings reproach. The leads share only wickedness, better, shame or leads, in unrelated prophetic and proverbial contexts.
  • Sirach 42:22: The unit exclaims how desirable all God's works are, visible like a spark. The psalms praise the greatness of God's works without the spark image or the desirability of the works, and the spark leads use the spark in unrelated images (fire, coals, reason).
  • Sirach 43:15: The unit says God strengthened the clouds and hailstones were broken in pieces. Job 38:22 and 37:6 speak of hail stored up and snow and rain commanded, and Joshua 10:11 of hailstones hurled in battle; none mentions strengthened clouds or broken hailstones. The remaining leads share only broken or strengthened.
  • Sirach 43:21: The unit says the ice of the north wind consumes mountains, burns the wilderness and extinguishes green growth like fire. Hosea 13:15 and Genesis 41:6 describe a scorching or blighting wind, and Isaiah 10:18 a fire of judgment; none attributes this burning effect to cold.
  • Sirach 44:2: The unit says the Lord created great glory, His majesty from of old, introducing the praise of famous men. Psalms 43:2-3 recalls God's deeds for the fathers, and the other leads use glory and majesty in general doxologies; none states this creation of glory.
  • Sirach 48:11: The unit blesses those who saw Elijah and those who fell asleep in love, and adds that we too will live. The leads use fallen asleep of Lazarus, the raised holy ones or witnesses of the risen Christ, without any reference to Elijah or this blessing.
  • Sirach 50:1: The unit names the high priest Simon son of Onias and his repair of the house. 2 Maccabees 3:1 names a later high priest Onias, and 2 Maccabees 4:1-4 a different Simon who opposed Onias, so neither is this Simon in this role. 2 Chronicles 34:10 and 1 Maccabees 9:62 describe other repairs.
  • Sirach 50:2: The unit credits Simon with a double wall and high retaining wall around the sacred precinct. The leads mention sacred precincts in other contexts (Israel's idolatry, a pagan temple, foreign altars, taxation) and not this construction.
  • Sirach 50:3: The unit records a reservoir hewn in Simon's days with a sea-like circumference. Deuteronomy and Nehemiah mention hewn cisterns the Israelites inherited, and Sirach 48:17 describes Hezekiah's reservoirs; none is this installation.
  • Sirach 50:4: The unit says Simon cared for his people against a fall and strengthened the city against siege. The leads use strengthen, fall or siege of other figures (Ezekiel's sign-act, Babylon, a Seleucid king) and do not describe this high priest's work.
  • Sirach 50:26: The unit names the inhabitants of Mount Samaria, the Philistines and the foolish people of Shechem as the hated nations. The leads mention Samaria, Samaritans, Philistines or Shechem in other contexts (resettlement, a boundary list, mourners, Jotham's speech, avoidance of Samaritans) but none shares this judgment on all three groups.
